# How far back do social media background checks go?

By Dave Fradette · Published September 26, 2026 · Last reviewed October 30, 2026

Short answer: Screening vendors like Checkr and Fama publicly describe a seven-year lookback for social media checks, though actual employer and vendor practices can vary. That window mirrors the seven-year limit the Fair Credit Reporting Act places on much of the adverse information in consumer reports.

Vendors describe lookbacks of up to seven years. PruneSocial reviews the last seven years of your own exports, privately, and shows what may deserve a second look. See a sample report or start a free preview. Don't have your export yet? Use the export checklist to request it, then come back. You can start with one platform and add the others later.

## The seven-year standard

Screening vendors that publish their lookback mostly land on seven years. Checkr describes a default seven-year lookback for its social media search, and Fama says its screening covers public content as far back as seven years. [1] [2] 

The number comes from the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Social media reports from a vendor are consumer reports, and the FCRA limits how long certain adverse information can appear in a consumer report, generally seven years, with exceptions such as criminal convictions and some higher-salary positions. [3] [2] Vendors that describe their lookback as "FCRA-aligned" are applying that same seven-year line to online content. [1] 

## What "seven years" means in practice

- It's counted back from the date of the check, so the window moves. A post from eight years ago is out, and one from six and a half years ago is in, but not for long.
- It applies to what you still have public. A post you deleted years ago generally isn't visible to a new check, but screenshots, archives, and reports that were already run can keep copies.
- Likes are a gray area. The date that matters is when you interacted, but not every platform records it. X's data export, for example, shows when the liked post was published, not when you liked it.
- Employers can still look on their own. The seven-year window is how vendors scope their reports. A recruiter who searches your name directly isn't bound by it.

## How to use this

1. Focus your cleanup on the last seven years. That's where the risk is concentrated.
2. Don't ignore older public posts entirely. They're outside a vendor's window, but still findable.
3. Pay attention to the recent end too. New posts and likes join the window every day, which is why a re-scan before each application is worth doing.

## Examples

| Rating | Example item | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear | A 2017 Instagram comment, whatever it says | Outside a seven-year window counted from 2026, so a vendor using that lookback wouldn't score it. |
| Consider | A 2020 Facebook post: "Hit 100 on the turnpike and didn't see a single cop." | Inside the window, and a first-person brag about reckless driving (Crime). |
| Consider | An X like with no like date, on a post about drug use | X doesn't record when you liked it, so a careful review treats it as possibly recent (Drugs). |

## How PruneSocial handles the window

PruneSocial scores only items from the last seven years and tells you how many older items it skipped. The one exception is X likes, which are always scored because the export has no like date. Your report also shows your scored items by year, so you can see where your history is concentrated. The full rules are in the methodology.

## Common questions

How far back do social media background checks go?

Screening vendors such as Checkr and Fama publicly describe a seven-year lookback for social media checks, though actual employer and vendor practices can vary.

Do older posts matter?

Posts outside a vendor's window are out of its report, but they can still be found. The seven-year window is how vendors scope their reports, and a recruiter who searches your name directly isn't bound by it.

Does the seven-year window apply to likes?

Likes are a gray area. The date that matters is when you interacted, but not every platform records it. X's data export shows when the liked post was published, not when you liked it, so PruneSocial always scores X likes.
